core_principles.text: Increasing the ankle abduction angle during the lunge exercise increases the muscle activity of the quadriceps femoris.
Performing the lunge with the ankle in a 60-degree abduction position can be used to selectively strengthen the vastus medialis oblique.
Adduction of the hip joint and the tibia during the lunge exercise helps strengthen the vastus medialis oblique.

specific_findings.text: In a study of 15 healthy male volunteers performing lunges at 0, 20, 40, and 60 degrees of ankle abduction, the most significantly increased muscle activity was observed in the vastus medialis oblique at 60 degrees of abduction.
A cited previous study demonstrated that the lunge exercise activated the vastus medialis oblique by 77% compared to other exercise schemes.

consequences.text: A weakened vastus medialis oblique relative to the vastus lateralis causes a muscle imbalance that pulls the patella excessively laterally, resulting in patellofemoral pain syndrome and chronic joint pain.
Failing to abduct the femur during the lunge increases pressure on the knee joint by failing to diminish the force delivered to the lateral patellofemoral joint.

source: data\lunge\Changes in lower limb muscle activity based on angle of ankle abduction during lunge exercise.pdf [part 1/3]

core_principles.text: To maintain stability during a lunge, look straight ahead and place your hands on your waist to prevent upper body sway.
Increasing the ankle abduction angle during a lunge can help to strengthen the quadriceps femoris muscle group.
Performing a lunge with an ankle abduction angle of 60 degrees is highly effective for selective strengthening of the vastus medialis oblique (VMO).

specific_findings.text: In a study of 15 healthy males, muscle activity of the rectus femoris (RF), vastus lateralis (VL), and vastus medialis oblique (VMO) significantly increased as ankle abduction angle increased from 0 to 60 degrees during a lunge.
At 0 degrees of ankle abduction, muscle activities were RF: 23.0 ± 12.8%, VL: 41.3 ± 20.9%, and VMO: 44.2 ± 24.0%.
At 60 degrees of ankle abduction, muscle activities reached their highest levels: RF: 37.6 ± 14.5%, VL: 57.0 ± 28.7%, and VMO: 63.6 ± 33.8%.
The VMO showed significantly higher levels of activity when the ankle abduction was 60 degrees compared to other angles (p<0.05).

source: data\lunge\Changes in lower limb muscle activity based on angle of ankle abduction during lunge exercise.pdf [part 2/3]
